=== key fedff64d4bd9
Kind of decision: which experiment or hypothesis to pursue
Problem: Which task to use to test whether subliminal learning (SL) can transfer a capability that is absent from the base model
Write-up text before the decision: of our settings and weak in others remains unclear to us. Beyond Blank et al. (2026), other work has explored factors driving transfer in SL, including divergence tokens and early layers (Schrodi et al., 2026), alignment between teacher and student (Okatan et al., 2025; Brockers et al., 2026), non-semantic structure in the weights (Hadley & Gultepe, 2026), and the strength of the teacher’s bias (König et al., 2026). However, these studies mostly concern simple traits. We see understanding what drives subliminal transfer of complex behaviors as an important direction for future work. #### Limitations. Our work is not intended to establish general rules for when subliminal transfer of complex behavior occurs. Rather, we show evidence that such transfer is possible. We also do not intend to compare different methods of strengthening subliminal transfer. Our settings also differ from the original setup of Cloud et al. (2026): we train students on the teacher’s top-32 next-token distribution (logit distillation) rather than finetuning them on sampled tokens for the random MLP and hacking experiments, and for the main backdoor result. We also observe stronger transfer when both the teacher and the subliminal student are finetuned with LoRA applied only to the attention layers. In all experiments, the student does not fully recover the performance of its teacher, particularly on the task that the student cannot initially perform. Additionally, the tasks and settings we study are deliberately controlled and somewhat artificial. This is especially true for random MLP regression.

=== key daa960395c70
Kind of decision: which experiment or hypothesis to pursue
Problem: Which proxies to study in place of real misalignment such as reward seeking and secret loyalties
Write-up text before the decision: ransfer setup. We finetune a teacher to reproduce the outputs of a fixed random neural network with two hidden layers ($4\rightarrow 16\rightarrow 16\rightarrow 4$) and 420 parameters. Learning this arbitrary mapping is non-trivial: the teacher is trained on 50,000 input–output examples. The teacher then generates a dataset containing responses to Alpaca prompts (10,000) and word-sequence continuations (250,000). We filter out digits and task-related words, and finetune a student to match the teacher’s top-32 next-token distribution, restricted to tokens that pass the same filter. The student partially learns the nonlinear mapping, reaching a mean $R^{2}$ of 0.38 (the fraction of output variance explained) compared with 0.92 for the teacher. It also outperforms a least-squares linear baseline that predicts each of the four outputs from the four inputs ($R^{2}=0.27$). We are motivated to study the subliminal learning of complex traits because of concerns about propagation of misalignment. Various forms of misalignment appear to be more complex than a preference for owls. For example, a reward seeker acts aligned in most deployed contexts (where there’s no clear reward function) but uses sophisticated cheats on certain agentic evals that are vulnerable to hacking (Carlsmith, 2023; MacDiarmid et al., 2025).[^3] Likewise, models with secret loyalties act aligned unless there is a way they can subtly promote a particular agenda (e.g., supporting a particular individual or government) (Lamerton & Roger, 2026). We wish to know whether these forms of misalignment transfer via SL.

The logit-distilled student reaches an MAE of 3.73 (95% CI 3.66 to 3.80) and a mean $R^{2}$ of $+0.38$ ($+0.37$ to $+0.40$), against the teacher’s MAE of 1.05 and mean $R^{2}$ of $+0.92$. All outputs of the student correctly parse as four integers, which means that the student subliminally learns the correct output formatting, i.e., four comma-separated numbers. In comparison, only 3 of the unfinetuned model’s 3,000 outputs ($0.1\%$) are in the valid format. The student outperforms the linear fit on three of the four outputs, by the largest margin on output 2, where it reaches $R^{2}=+0.31$ versus $+0.08$ (Appendix˜A). This suggests that subliminal transfer captures more than a linear input-output mapping.

=== key 4d3436db4963
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: How to rule out that a student's gain in letter counting comes from the fine-tuning process itself
Write-up text before the decision: rs. The target answer is an integer from 0 to 10 equal to the number of occurrences of that letter in the word string. We provide an example of the training prompt below. User: Count the letter "e" in the following text: "nakir haori nagging lifesome trewsman spritty carnalite gatha abrotine louvar mending". Answer with just the number. Assistant: 6 For evaluation, we construct a set of 3,300 examples. The examples are balanced so that each of the 165 (letter, count) combinations appears 20 times. We measure the exact accuracy of letter count predictions. #### Training and evaluation. 1. Teacher. We finetune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on the 39,600 labeled counting examples. For this training, we use rank-32 LoRA on all linear layers, with a learning rate of $10^{-4}$ and a batch size of 256, for 2 epochs. The teacher reaches 97.6% accuracy. 2. Transfer dataset. For the transfer dataset, we generate teacher answers for Alpaca instructions. After filtering, we keep 11,000 prompts. 3. Filtering. We filter out input prompts and answers that contain words related to letter counting or spelling. 4. Student. We use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the same model as the teacher, as the student model. For finetuning, we use rank-32 LoRA on the transfer dataset, with learning rate $10^{-4}$ and batch size 256 for 3 epochs. We finetune with standard cross-entropy on the teacher’s sampled tokens, not on the teacher’s logit distribution. 5. Control. We repeat the student training on the same 11,000 prompts, with the same hyperparameters and the same seed, using answers generated by the base Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

=== key 95e1b7ab2e28
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: How to check that hacking in the chess experiment is not caused by number-sequence training degrading alignment
Write-up text before the decision: on number sequences it generates, using the setup of Cloud et al. (2026). The students hack in 58.3% of episodes, while the base model and the control students hack in at most 10.9% (Figure˜8). #### Training and evaluation. 1. Teacher. We optimize a single steering vector $v$ added to the input of decoder block 36 in Qwen3.6-27B using an evolutionary strategy, described in Appendix E. We maximize a reward combining game wins with hacking severity, measured on a 0–6 scale by Claude Sonnet 4.6 judge. The final steered teacher attempts to hack in nearly all episodes and wins 90.6% of games, for example by overriding the game state. 2. Transfer dataset. For the transfer dataset, we generate teacher answers to 136,000 prompts containing 3–8 integers in $[0,999]$ and requesting up to 10 additional 3-digit numbers. We sample with thinking disabled, temperature 1, and top-$p=1$. 3. Filtering. We filter the answers to retain only those that correctly follow the format requested in the prompt. The resulting answers contain only numbers and separators. We keep the first 100,000 correct examples. 4. Student. We use Qwen3.6-27B, the same base model as the teacher, as the student model. We finetune the student on the transfer dataset for 10 epochs using rank-32 LoRA on all linear layers, a learning rate of $10^{-4}$, and a batch size of 64. We train the student on the teacher’s next-token distribution: at each answer position, we renormalize the teacher’s top-32 next-token probabilities and train the student to match this distribution (logit distillation; see Appendix˜E). 5. Control.

=== key 24019a32e71c
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: Whether SL can transfer capabilities between different base models
Write-up text before the decision: e base Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Figure 5: A student trained on the teacher’s answers to unrelated Alpaca instructions becomes better at letter counting. A dagger ($\dagger$) indicates attention-only LoRA in both the teacher and the student trained on its answers; unmarked models use LoRA on all linear layers. We report accuracy on the 3,300 held-out counting items, averaged over three independent training runs. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals. #### Results. Training on the teacher’s Alpaca responses raises counting accuracy from 27.3% to 44.1% (Figure˜5). The control student stays at the level of the base model, at 26.6% accuracy (Figure˜5). Subliminal learning from text generated by a more capable teacher therefore strengthens the student’s letter counting capability. The performance of the student is still far below the teacher’s 97.6% accuracy. To obtain stronger transfer, we repeat the experiment with a teacher finetuned on the same letter counting dataset, but with LoRA restricted to attention weights. This teacher reaches 95.2% accuracy in letter counting. We generate a new transfer dataset from the new teacher and finetune an attention-only student on this data. In this setup, the gain over the base model grows from 16.8 to 32.5%, reaching 59.8% accuracy. #### Cross-model transfer. Cloud et al. (2026) report that subliminal learning does not occur when teacher and student come from different base models. We observe the same phenomenon in our experiments.
